e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the place named Beth Horon, rendered as “Beth” and “Horon.” It functions as a proper place name rather than a description of an action, quality, or person. The name occurs 28 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Joshua, and appears in geographical and military settings. Scripture also connects Beth Horon with routes and territorial boundaries, showing that it identifies a recognized location in the land. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes something as “old,” emphasizing that it has become aged or longstanding. It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three verses: twice each in Joshua 9:4 and Joshua 9:5, and once in Ezekiel 23:43. Its normal meaning is therefore a straightforward description of age or worn time, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew verb describes breaking or making a breach—something being opened, split, or broken through. It can describe a physical opening, such as waters breaking apart, and can also express a breach or rupture in a broader situation. The word occurs 51 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on what is being broken or opened in each passage. Its central idea remains a forceful breaking through or dividing apart.

It is a Hebrew noun meaning “treasurers,” the people designated by that title. The word names those referred to as treasurers rather than describing an action, quality, or place. In the Hebrew Bible corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:21. Its basic sense is therefore a title or designation for treasurers; the surrounding verse supplies the particular responsibilities or setting intended there.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “stranger” or “foreigner”—a person living among a people without being native to them. It is used broadly in the Old Testament, appearing 92 times, especially in laws and instructions concerning how such people are to be treated. The word can describe someone residing within Israel, and Scripture repeatedly places this person within matters of justice, protection, worship, and communal responsibility. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “falling,” describing someone or something going down rather than remaining upright. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Psalms. In the available English rendering, it is translated “falling” each time. Its precise force in either psalm depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea is the state or action of falling.

This word means “that,” pointing to something already identified or distinguished in the surrounding sentence. It is a demonstrative expression, so its meaning depends on the person, thing, or situation being indicated by the context. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 36:35. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the specific thing it points to cannot be identified from the word alone.

e.t: Harum is a personal name, rendered “Harum.” It identifies a person in the genealogy recorded at 1 Chronicles 4:8. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and its only recorded occurrence is in that genealogy. The available material supports understanding it as a name rather than as a general description or action word. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text.

This Hebrew verb means “dwell”: to live or remain in a place. It expresses the act of making one’s residence somewhere rather than merely passing through. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 30:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic idea is settled residence or continued presence. The word therefore points to inhabiting a place and being established there.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “age,” especially the condition of being advanced in years or old. It describes a person’s later stage of life rather than a specific number of years. In its four Old Testament occurrences, all in Genesis, it is used of people whose age is relevant to the account. The surrounding wording determines whether English renders the idea as age or old, but the central sense remains a person’s advanced years.

“Haggiah” is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 6:30. Because the available rendering preserves it as a name and no broader definition is provided, its main meaning is its role as a person’s name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that individual’s place in the passage.

e.t: The word means “galbanum,” functioning as the name of a particular substance. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Exodus 30:34. In that occurrence, the word serves as an object connected with what is spoken and with taking or preparing it, so it identifies something being referred to rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in the verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is the substance named “galbanum.”

e.t: This Hebrew word means “vinegar,” the name of a concrete liquid mentioned in Old Testament sentences. It functions as a noun: it can be treated as an item associated with eating or drinking, and it may appear as something given. The word occurs six times in five Old Testament verses, from Numbers through Proverbs, with “vinegar” as its consistent meaning.

This Hebrew word means “clay,” referring to the earthy material itself. It names a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all within seven verses of Daniel 2, so its recorded use is concentrated in one passage. The repeated rendering “clay” supports this straightforward material meaning, while the surrounding verse explains its particular significance there.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “want,” describing a condition in which something needed is lacking. It functions as the thing spoken of in passages where God gives or sends this condition. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Deuteronomy and once in Amos. Its meaning remains centered on deprivation or insufficiency, while the surrounding passage determines what is lacking and why it is being described.

This Hebrew word refers to magicians: people recognized in the royal courts of Babylon for practicing or claiming special wisdom and supernatural arts. It is a title or designation for a group, not a general word for ordinary wisdom or learning. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, where it identifies court figures consulted by kings about troubling matters and dreams. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense is a magician or member of such a courtly class.

This Hebrew word refers to a person named “Ahi,” functioning as a personal name rather than a general description or action. It occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 7:34. The available passages identify the same rendered name, but without their verse text, no further contextual meaning should be added. e.t: This Hebrew noun means “hand.” It functions as a noun referring to a hand. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it appears in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Psalms. Its uses include descriptions of physical dimensions and a poetic statement in Psalm 39:5, but the surrounding verse determines the precise force there. The word’s basic reference remains the same, while the sentence determines how that reference is being used.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, not a common term whose ordinary meaning can be translated from the available information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:47. No explicit definition, gloss, or approved meaning clue is available, so its precise name meaning should not be supplied. The reference identifies where the name appears, but without the verse text it does not establish any further significance or description.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Jonadab.” It identifies people named Jonadab rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs seven times, across six verses, in 2 Samuel and Jeremiah. The name refers to individuals appearing in those passages, including a Jonadab associated with David’s family and a Jonadab connected with the Rechabites. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage and the person being identified.

Japhleti is an identifying Hebrew name or designation, rendered “Japhleti.” It functions as a specific label rather than a general description such as an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 16:3, so its ordinary scriptural use is limited to that single occurrence. Without the verse text, its precise referent cannot be described more narrowly.

e.t: This word means “pins,” referring to small pointed pieces used to secure or hold something in place. It functions as a noun and commonly describes practical objects connected with tents, furnishings, or other structures. The word occurs 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent physical sense rather than an abstract idea. Its uses also include imagery of something firmly established or fastened, but the ordinary meaning remains pins used for securing.

This Hebrew word is the place name “Chezib,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word with a stated definition. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 38:5, and is rendered “Chezib” in the available English renderings. Because no short definition is preserved, its clearest meaning is its role as a proper name identifying a place. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what happens there or why the place matters.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to something given in exchange, especially a ransom or payment that answers for a person or obligation. It commonly appears with the idea of giving something “for” another, and “ransom” expresses that exchange more specifically. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, including laws and passages about deliverance, repayment, and what is offered to meet a required cost. The exact sense in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the exchange.

e.t: This Hebrew word functions as “the,” marking a noun as definite rather than referring to it generally. It appears nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across Deuteronomy, Job, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its role is grammatical: it helps identify or specify the noun it accompanies. The surrounding words determine exactly what is being identified in each passage, so its force belongs with the complete sentence rather than standing alone.

e.t: Midian is the name “Midian,” used to identify a people or place in the Hebrew Scriptures. It appears 59 times in the Old Testament, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Habakkuk. The name occurs in genealogical settings and later in accounts involving conflict and commands concerning Midian. Its use therefore identifies a specific biblical people or territory rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word refers to “bands,” describing strips or cords used to bind or hold something together. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 38:31. Since no broader lexical definition or repeated usage is available, its clearest supported sense remains a physical binding or fastening material. Its precise force in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself points to bands rather than an action or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word refers to “lurking” or a “place.” Its two Old Testament occurrences show that it can be understood either as the act of remaining hidden or as the location associated with that concealment. Because no short definition is supplied, these two established renderings provide the clearest lexical sense. The word appears once in 1 Samuel 23:23 and once in Isaiah 32:2, so its precise emphasis depends on how the surrounding sentence uses it.

This Hebrew verb means to escape or get away from danger, pursuit, or a threatening situation. It describes a person or group successfully avoiding capture, harm, or death. The word occurs 95 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it expresses a recurring biblical idea of deliverance through getting away. Its exact emphasis—whether flight, survival, or release—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “son,” referring to a male child or descendant. It functions as a noun, naming the person connected to another by family or descent. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Proverbs 29:21. Because it appears only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its broader significance in that passage should be understood from the full context rather than from the word alone.

This Hebrew word means “scab,” referring to a crusted skin condition examined by the priest in Leviticus 13. It is a noun used for the visible condition itself, especially as the priest determined whether the affected area had changed and whether the person should be regarded as clean or unclean. The word occurs three times, all in Leviticus 13:6–8, and each occurrence is rendered “scab.”

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears 43 times, often in passages addressing the deeds of people or nations before God. Its use can point to either faithful or blameworthy conduct, so the surrounding sentence determines how those doings are viewed.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “nails,” referring to pointed objects used for fastening or securing something. It functions as a concrete noun and appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Ecclesiastes 12:11. Its recorded use is connected with an object being given or placed, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular force of that occurrence. The word’s basic meaning remains a physical nail or fastening spike.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “butler.” It functions as a designation for a person holding a household or court service role, rather than as an action or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, with many occurrences in Genesis and later references connected with royal settings. Its use identifies an official serving in a household or court. The surrounding verse determines the precise setting, but the central meaning remains “butler.”

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Eleasah.” It identifies people in the Old Testament rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears six times in six verses, chiefly in genealogical records in 1 Chronicles, and also in Ezra and Jeremiah. In the genealogies, Eleasah is presented as a person connected with family descent and birth relationships. The supplied material does not provide a separate lexical definition for the name, so its supported meaning here is its use as the proper name Eleasah.

This Hebrew word refers to a “prophet,” a person identified by that designation. The plural rendering “prophets” refers to more than one such person. Its basic meaning is therefore a title or description for a prophet, rather than an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs eight times, all within Ezra, showing its use in references to one or more prophets in that book.

Nahum is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Nahum” in the one Old Testament occurrence represented by this word. It identifies the person named in Nahum 1:1 rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Readers should therefore understand it first as the individual’s name. Because this word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament record, its precise significance as a name is not established here beyond that personal-name function.

e.t: This Hebrew word functions in the sentence as “the,” marking a definite expression rather than supplying a broad descriptive idea by itself. It appears twice in the Old Testament, once in Judges 16:9 and once in Isaiah 1:31. Its precise contribution depends on the noun or phrase it accompanies in each verse. As a small grammatical word, it helps identify something definite within the sentence rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract concept on its own.

This Hebrew word refers to openings in rock or the ground—“clefts” or “holes.” It names a physical place or opening rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Isaiah and Jeremiah, and its repeated renderings point consistently to a hollow or fissure where something may be located, concealed, or sent. Its exact force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a cleft, cavity, or hole in the landscape.

This Hebrew word means “letter,” referring to a written message or official document. In its three Old Testament occurrences, all in Ezra, it names a document used for written communication. As a noun, it identifies the letter itself rather than the act of writing or the person who sends it. The surrounding passage determines who sent it and what issue it addressed, while the word’s basic meaning remains “letter.”

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, Ebed-melech, referring to an individual in Jeremiah’s account. It is not presented here with an explicit common-word definition or English rendering, so its normal use is best understood as identifying this person rather than describing an action or quality. The name occurs twelve times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all within Jeremiah 38–39, where it appears in connections involving the king’s commands, movement, and danger. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding text.

This Hebrew word means “chaff,” functioning as a noun that names the material identified by that term. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Daniel 2:35, so its normal biblical usage is represented by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. The word itself identifies chaff as the subject being described; the precise force of that description belongs to the surrounding verse and passage.

Azzan is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, and its English rendering is “Azzan.” The name occurs in Numbers 34:26, in a passage that identifies people connected with Israel’s tribal leadership. Without the surrounding verse text, no further meaning or role should be assigned to the name itself. Its normal function is simply to identify this individual.

This Hebrew word means “the.” It serves as a definite article, marking a person or thing as a particular, known one rather than an unspecified one. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs four times, all in Daniel 7. Because no verse text is provided, its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding words. It is not best treated as an independent description or action, but as a small word that makes a noun definite.

This Hebrew word describes something as “strong,” emphasizing strength or great power. It appears 31 times in the Old Testament, showing that it is used in varied settings rather than being a rare or specialized term. The word functions as a describing word, applying “strong” to whatever person, people, or thing the sentence discusses. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains “strong.”

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise ordinary meaning cannot be securely stated from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 18:7. The reference identifies its location, but no explicit definition, approved meaning clue, or verse text is available here to clarify what it names or expresses. Its role therefore must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from this word record alone.

Pedaiah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Pedaiah” in English. It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or teaching. The name occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, referring to individuals mentioned in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Because it is a name, its meaning in a particular passage comes from the person being identified and the surrounding account, not from a general concept carried by the word itself.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a concubine, a woman recognized in a household relationship with a man but distinct from a full wife. It is used in genealogies and narrative accounts, showing that the word can identify women connected with families and their children as well as women involved in household events. The word occurs 37 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Judges, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles.

This Hebrew verb means “divide,” expressing the action of separating something into parts. In its Old Testament usage, it appears 14 times, especially in passages describing distinctions among animals according to their bodily features. It can function as an action attributed to an animal or as a description of something already divided. Its central idea remains the making of a distinction or separation, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is being divided.

e.t: Zibia is a personal name, rendered “Zibia” in English. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:9, within a genealogy. The name functions as the identity of a woman connected with the birth of a son, so it identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its precise personal significance is not stated in the biblical text, and the available passage does not provide a separate definition or description of the name.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “shade.” It identifies shade as a place or condition associated with shelter, covering, or relief from direct sunlight. Scripture uses it in descriptions of physical shade and in poetic language connected with protection and dependence. It occurs 49 times in the Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Jonah. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word is the name “Zoar,” referring to a place in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences in Genesis and later mentions in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The cited references consistently render it “Zoar,” identifying that particular place.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Zipporah.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, referring to the same named woman. The surrounding SEE relationships present her as connected with marriage and family, while other passages associate her with giving and speech. The word’s basic meaning is therefore its identifying role as a woman’s name, and its precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s context.

The Hebrew word means “lie.” It functions as a noun, naming a thing or condition in a sentence rather than expressing an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Job, at Job 37:8 and Job 38:40. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical idea is the noun “lie.”

This Hebrew verb means to “lament” or be “lamented”—to express sorrow openly, especially in mourning. It describes vocal or public grief over death and loss rather than quiet sadness alone. In the Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including accounts of David’s mourning and descriptions of professional mourners. The word functions as an action: someone laments, or sorrow is expressed for someone who has died. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb means “cut.” It expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Daniel 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic lexical sense remains the act of cutting. The English rendering is consistently “cut,” supporting this straightforward meaning without requiring additional senses or broader translation alternatives.

This Hebrew verb means “hardened”: it describes becoming firm, stubborn, or resistant rather than responsive. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, once in Job and once in Isaiah. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition involving hardening. In Isaiah, it is connected with the Lord and with matters involving the heart, inheritance, and tribes, showing that the word can describe a hardened disposition in relation to God and his people. The surrounding verse determines the precise force, but its central idea remains becoming hardened or unyielding.

This Hebrew word refers to “drunkenness”—the condition of being drunk. It is used as a descriptive noun for that condition rather than as a command or action word. The Hebrew Old Testament records three occurrences, appearing once each in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains drunkenness.

Raamiah is a personal name, rendered “Raamiah,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears once, in Nehemiah 7:7, and serves to identify an individual in the Hebrew text. It is not presented here as a term with an explained abstract sense. Its ordinary function is therefore as a person’s name; the surrounding verse would be needed for any further contextual detail.

This Hebrew word means “well,” referring to a place or structure from which water is obtained. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 24:5. In that sentence, it functions as the object connected with the action being described. Because this word occurs only once and no verse text is available here, its broader range cannot be established beyond this basic meaning. Its recorded rendering supports understanding it as a well rather than as an action or quality.

Sibmah is a proper place name, rendered “Sibmah” in the Old Testament. It identifies a location mentioned among places associated with Israel’s territorial inheritance and later prophetic references. The name occurs six times in six Old Testament verses, from Numbers through Jeremiah. Because it functions as a name rather than a descriptive term, its precise significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word describes someone as “grayheaded,” referring to the visible signs of advanced age. It functions as a descriptive word applied to a person rather than naming an object or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 12:2 and once in Job 15:10. Its basic sense remains focused on gray hair or a gray head as an age-related description.

Meron is a Hebrew proper name, identifying a particular person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. It is best understood as a name to be recognized, not translated into a descriptive English word. This name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with both occurrences appearing in Joshua 12:20. Its precise referent belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a distinctive name.

e.t: Serug is a personal name, referring to an individual in the family line recorded in Genesis and later listed in 1 Chronicles. It is not presented here as a general Hebrew word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly within the genealogy of Abraham’s ancestors. Its scriptural use consistently identifies the same named figure in that lineage.

This Hebrew word expresses the number “threescore.” It functions as a numerical quantity, indicating how many of something are being counted rather than describing a person, place, action, or quality. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in three verses recorded in Ezra and Daniel. Its use is therefore specific and numerical, with the same basic sense throughout its occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “hope.” It names something a person looks toward or waits for, functioning as the object of expectation in a sentence. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Lamentations. Its use across these writings presents hope as something that may be held, placed before a person, or lost. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to a bright or noticeably light mark on the skin. It is used in Leviticus in descriptions of visible skin conditions that a priest was to examine. The word functions as a noun naming the bright appearance itself, rather than describing the priest’s judgment or the person’s complete condition. It occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Leviticus 13–14, where careful observation of such marks is part of the instructions concerning skin disease and cleansing.
